source_text:
Quam pulchrum spectaculum Deo, cum Christianus cum dolore congreditur, cum aduersum minas et supplicia et tormenta componitur, cum strepitum mortis et horrorem carnificis inridens inculcat, cum libertatem suam aduersus reges et principes erigit, soli Deo, cuius est, cedit, cum triumphator et uictor ipsi, qui aduersum se sententiam dixit, insultat! uicit enim qui quod contendit obtinuit.
quis non miles sub oculis imperatoris audacius periculum prouocet? nemo enim praemium percipit ante experimentum. et imperator tamen quod non habet, non dat: non potest propagare uitam, potest honestare militiam.
at enim Dei miles nec in dolore deseritur nec morte finitur. sic Christianus miser uideri potest, non potest inueniri. uos ipsi calamitosos uiros fertis ad caelum, Mucium Scaeuolam, qui cum errasset in regem perisset in hostibus, nisi dexteram perdidisset.
et quot ex nostris, non dextram solum, sed totum corpus uri, cremari sine ullis eiulatibus pertulerunt, cum dimitti praesertim haberent in sua potestate!
uiros cumMucio uel cum Aquilio aut Regulo comparo? pueri et mulierculae nostrae cruces et tormenta, feras et omnes suppliciorum terriculas inspirata patientia doloris inludunt.
nec intellegitis o miseri, neminem esse qui aut sine ratione uelit poenam subire aut tormenta sine Deo possit sustinere:
nisi forte uos decipit, quod Deum nescientes diuitiis afluant, honoribus floreant, polleant potestatibus. miseri in hoc altius tolluntur, ut decidant altius. hi enim ut uictimae ad supplicium saginantur, ut hostiae ad poenam coronantur: in hoc adeo quidam imperiis ac dominationibus eriguntur, ut ingenium eorum perditae mentes licentia potestatis libere nundinentur.
absque enim notitia Dei quae potest esse solida felicitas, cum mors sit? somnio similis antequam tenetur, elabitur. rex es?
sed tam times quam timeris, et quamlibet sis multo comitatu stipatus, ad periculum tamen solus es. diues es ? sed fortunae male creditur et magno uiatico breue uitae iter non instruitur, sed oneratur.
fascibus et purpuris gloriaris? uanus error hominis et inanis cultus dignitatis, fulgere purpura, mente sordescere. nobilitate generosus es? parentes tuos laudas? omnes tamen pari sorte nascimur, sola uirtute distinguimur.
nos igitur, qui moribus et pudore censemur, merito malis uoluptatibus et pompis uestris et spectaculis. abstinemus, quorum et de sacris originem nouimus et noxia blandimenta damnamus. nam in ludis currulibus quis non horreat populi in se rixantis insaniam? in gladiatoriis homicidii disciplinam?
in scenicis etiam non minor furor et turpitudo prolixior: nunc enim mimus uel exponit adulteria uel monstrat, nunc eneruis histrio amorem dum fingit, infligit: idem deos uestros induendo stupra, suspiria, odia dedecorat, idem simulatis doloribus lacrimas uestras uanis gestibus et nutibus prouocat: sic homicidium in uero flagitatis, in mendacio fletis.
thought_title: The Christian as conqueror and the emptiness of worldly goods
orientation: Octavius is still answering Caecilius, now showing that Christians endure torture as victors and that pagan wealth and rank are empty.
pass_a_gloss: How beautiful [a] spectacle [to] God, when [a] Christian with pain contends, when against threats and punishments and tortures he is arrayed, when [the] din of death and [the] horror of [the] executioner ridiculing he tramples, when his freedom against kings and princes he raises, [to] God alone, whose he is, he yields, when [as] triumphator and victor [over] him who against him [the] sentence spoke, he insults! For he has conquered who what he contended [for] has obtained. What soldier not under [the] eyes of [his] commander more boldly [would] danger provoke? For no one [a] reward receives before [the] test. And [the] commander nevertheless what he does not have, does not give: he cannot prolong life, he can honor [military] service. But indeed [the] soldier of God neither in pain is abandoned nor by death is ended. Thus [a] Christian wretched [to] seem can, [but] cannot be found [so]. You yourselves [as] calamitous men carry [up] to heaven, Mucius Scaevola, who when he had erred against [the] king would have perished among [the] enemies, unless [his] right hand he had lost. And how many of ours, not [the] right hand only, but [the] whole body to be burned, to be cremated without any wailings endured, when to be released especially they had in their own power! Men with Mucius or with Aquilius or Regulus do I compare? Boys and little women of ours crosses and tortures, beasts and all [the] scarecrows of punishments [with] inspired patience of pain mock. Nor do you understand, O wretched [men], [that] no one is who either without reason would wish punishment to undergo or tortures without God could endure: unless perhaps you [it] deceives, that [those] not knowing God [with] riches abound, [with] honors flourish, [are] strong [in] powers. Wretched [men] for this [reason] higher are lifted, so that they may fall [from] higher. For these as victims for punishment are fattened, as sacrificial animals for penalty are crowned: for this [reason] indeed some [men] to commands and dominations are raised, so that [the] disposition of their ruined minds [by] license of power freely may be trafficked. For without knowledge of God what can be solid happiness, when death is? [To] a dream similar before it is grasped, it slips away. [A] king are you? But as much you fear as you are feared, and however much you may be [with] [a] great retinue surrounded, for danger nevertheless alone you are. Rich are you? But [to] fortune badly it is trusted and [with] [a] great travel-provision [the] short journey of life is not equipped, but burdened. [In] fasces and purple do you glory? [A] vain error of man and empty cultivation of rank, to gleam [in] purple, [in] mind to be filthy. [By] nobility well-born are you? [Your] parents do you praise? All nevertheless [with] equal lot are born, [by] virtue alone are we distinguished. We therefore, who by morals and modesty are assessed, deservedly [from] evil pleasures and your processions and spectacles abstain, of which both from [their] sacred rites [the] origin we know and [their] harmful allurements we condemn. For in chariot games who would not shudder at [the] madness of [the] people quarreling among themselves? In gladiatorial [games] [at] [the] training in homicide? In stage [shows] also not less [is] [the] fury and [the] baseness more prolonged: for now [the] mime either exposes adulteries or shows [them], now [the] effeminate actor love while he feigns, inflicts [it]: [the] same [man] your gods by putting on [their] debaucheries, sighs, hatreds disgraces, [the] same [man] [with] feigned griefs your tears [with] empty gestures and nods provokes: thus homicide in reality you demand, [over] [it] in falsehood you weep.

choices.term: cum strepitum mortis et horrorem carnificis inridens inculcat
choices.english: when he tramples on the din of death and the executioner's horror with mockery
choices.why: inculcat means to tread or trample underfoot; keeping the physical verb preserves the image of contemptuous triumph
rejected: when he scorns the noise of death and the dread of the executioner

choices.why: mulierculae is a diminutive, and the pairing with pueri stresses the weakness of those who endure; 'little women' keeps the diminutive force
terricula is a rare diminutive meaning objects of terror; 'scarecrows' conveys both the diminutive and the contempt
inspirata suggests divinely breathed-in patience; 'inspired' keeps the passive participle and the divine implication
perditae means destroyed or ruined; 'ruined' keeps the moral force of the participle
nundinor means to trade or traffic; the commercial metaphor is deliberate and should be kept

pass_b_english: What a beautiful sight for God when a Christian grapples with pain, when he stands arrayed against threats, punishments, and tortures, when, laughing, he drives home the din of death and the executioner's horror, when he raises his freedom against kings and rulers and yields only to God, whose he is, when he taunts the very man who pronounced sentence against him as a conqueror and victor! For he has won who has obtained what he fought for.

What soldier would not court danger more boldly under his commander's eyes? No one receives a reward before the test. And yet a commander cannot give what he does not have: he cannot prolong life, but he can honor military service.

But God's soldier is neither abandoned in pain nor ended by death. So a Christian can seem wretched, but he cannot be found wretched. You yourselves carry calamitous men to heaven: Mucius Scaevola, who would have perished among the enemy if he had offended the king, had he not lost his right hand.
And how many of our people have endured not only their right hand but their whole body being burned and cremated without any wailings, especially when they had it in their own power to be released!
Do I compare men with Mucius or with Aquilius or Regulus? Our boys and little women mock crosses and tortures, wild beasts and all the terrors of punishment, with inspired endurance of pain.
Do you not understand, you wretched people, that no one either wants to undergo punishment without reason or can endure tortures without God?

Unless perhaps you are deceived because those who do not know God overflow with riches, flourish with honors, and are strong in positions of power. Wretched people are lifted higher for this reason: so that they may fall from higher. For they are fattened like victims for punishment, crowned like sacrificial animals for the penalty. Indeed, some are raised to commands and dominions for this purpose: so that their ruined minds may freely traffic in the license of power.

For without knowledge of God, what happiness can be solid, since death exists? Like a dream, it slips away before it is grasped. Are you a king? You fear as much as you are feared, and however much you are surrounded by a large retinue, you are still alone when danger comes. Are you rich? Fortune is badly trusted, and the short journey of life is not equipped but weighed down by a large travel allowance.

Do you glory in fasces and purple? It is the empty error of a human being and the hollow cultivation of rank to gleam in purple while the mind is filthy. Are you noble by birth? Do you praise your parents? We are all born with equal lot; we are distinguished by virtue alone.

We, therefore, who are judged by our character and modesty, rightly abstain from your evil pleasures, your processions, and your spectacles. We know the origin of these things from your sacred rites, and we condemn their harmful allurements. For in chariot races, who would not shudder at the madness of the people fighting among themselves? In gladiatorial games, at the training in homicide?

In the theater there is no less frenzy and more prolonged shame. Now the mime either exposes or demonstrates adulteries; now the effeminate actor inflicts love while he feigns it. The same man disgraces your gods by dressing them in debauchery, sighs, and hatreds; the same man provokes your tears with feigned grief and empty gestures and nods. So you demand homicide in reality, and you weep over it in fiction.

problems.why: Latin says “terrible punishments,” not “scarecrows of punishments.”
problems.ruling: terriculas means 'frightful things/bugbears,' not 'scarecrows'; 'terrible punishments' misreads the diminutive plural form.

fixed: Changed 'scarecrows of punishments' to 'terrors of punishment': source 'suppliciorum terriculas' means 'terrors of punishments' (terricula = 'frightening things, terrors'), not 'scarecrows.'

problems.quote: who would have perished among the enemy if he had missed the king, had he not lost his right hand
problems.source_quote: qui cum errasset in regem perisset in hostibus, nisi dexteram perdidisset
problems.why: Latin says "errasset in regem" (offended/attacked the king), not "missed the king".
problems.fix: who would have perished among the enemy if he had offended the king, had he not lost his right hand

problems.quote: when he tramples with mockery on the din of death and the executioner's horror
problems.source_quote: cum strepitum mortis et horrorem carnificis inridens inculcat
problems.why: inculcat means 'presses in, drives home,' not 'tramples'; inridens modifies the subject (he mocks), not the action
problems.fix: when, laughing, he drives home the din of death and the executioner's horror
problems.ruling: inculcat = 'presses in', not 'tramples'; inridens modifies subject, not action

last_rejected.fix: who would have perished among the enemy if he had missed his aim at the king
last_rejected.ruling: errasset = erred/offended the king, translation conveys sense

last_rejected.quote: when they had it in their own power to be released
last_rejected.source_quote: cum dimitti praesertim haberent in sua potestate
last_rejected.why: dimitti means 'to be let go/acquitted', not 'released' from torture specifically
last_rejected.fix: especially when they had it in their own power to be let go
last_rejected.ruling: dimitti = to be let go/released, translation fits

last_rejected.why: inspirata here means 'breathed into/infused by God', not 'inspired' in modern sense

last_rejected.quote: no one either wants to undergo punishment without reason
last_rejected.source_quote: neminem esse qui aut sine ratione uelit poenam subire
last_rejected.why: sine ratione means 'without a rational cause/motive', not 'without reason' as in pointlessly
last_rejected.fix: no one either wants to undergo punishment without a rational cause
last_rejected.ruling: sine ratione = without rational cause, “without reason” matches

last_rejected.quote: the empty error of a human being and the hollow cultivation of rank
last_rejected.source_quote: uanus error hominis et inanis cultus dignitatis
last_rejected.why: hominis is genitive singular 'of a human', but 'human being' is awkward; 'man's empty delusion' better
last_rejected.fix: man's empty delusion and hollow cultivation of rank
last_rejected.ruling: error hominis = man's error, cultus dignitatis = cultivation of rank, translation adequate

last_rejected.why: prolixior means 'more extensive/widespread', not 'more prolonged' in time
last_rejected.fix: no less frenzy and more extensive shame

last_rejected.quote: the effeminate actor inflicts love while he feigns it
last_rejected.source_quote: eneruis histrio amorem dum fingit, infligit
last_rejected.why: infligit here means 'inflicts (love) on the audience', but 'inflicts love' is nonsensical; he arouses/inflicts passion
last_rejected.fix: the effeminate actor arouses passion while he feigns it

last_rejected.quote: So you demand homicide in reality, and you weep over it in fiction
last_rejected.source_quote: sic homicidium in uero flagitatis, in mendacio fletis
last_rejected.why: flagitatis means 'demand as a right/cry out for', stronger than 'demand'; 'in uero' is 'in truth/reality'
last_rejected.fix: So you cry out for homicide in reality, and weep over it in falsehood
last_rejected.ruling: flagitatis = demand/cry for, “demand” captured in translation

last_rejected.quote: yields only to God, whose he is
last_rejected.why: Agency reversed; Latin says he yields to the only God, to whom it belongs, not that the Christian is God's.
last_rejected.fix: yields only to the one God to whom he belongs
last_rejected.ruling: "cuius est" = "whose he is"; "soli Deo" = "to God alone/only"; both readings valid.

last_rejected.quote: weighed down by a large travel allowance
last_rejected.source_quote: magno viatico breue vitae iter non instruitur, sed oneratur
last_rejected.why: Latin says the short life journey is not provided with a great provision but is burdened; English adds a large allowance, opposite meaning.
last_rejected.fix: not provided with a great provision, but is burdened
last_rejected.ruling: "magno viatico" = "by/with a large travel provision/allowance"; English captures Latin accurately.
